doc.title: Bob Havens interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Childhood in Quincy: records and the family piano
summary: Born in Quincy, Illinois; his mother's music-store samples, the wind-up victrola with Whiteman records, and evenings at the piano with his parents.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: That’s right. I was born in Quincy, Illinois.
Can you recall, as a child, what the first kinds of music that made an impression on you were?

Well when I was quite young, well I would go back probably to my grade school years, the first thing I remember musically is my mother used to work at a music store and she sold sheet music and records. And during that time she brought home a lot of samples, like old recordings — these would date back into the twenties. And that’s the first thing I remember is having this wind-up victrola in the home. It was considered a console model, where you put the record on the top and the sound came out the bottom through an inside horn. So we always had these records in our attic area. And I would go up to the attic and bring down a stack of records and I would just put them on one by one. And I would say mostly it was recordings of large orchestras, such as Paul Whiteman and the Benson Orchestra of Chicago. I’m just naming names that come to me, it probably doesn’t mean

anything to anybody nowadays, and Charlie Straight was another orchestra that I listened to. And I became acquainted with the dance orchestras of the time by just playing these records. And of course at that time I wasn’t particularly — my mind wasn’t directed toward jazz at any particular amount at that time, and I was just becoming acquainted with music. I did it by records. But another fortunate thing was that my mother and father were both musical. And we had a family ritual, after an evening meal we would gather around the family piano and my mother played the piano, and she would get a big stack of music and just start pulling out things and playing and I would listen and sort of sing along at that time, until I reached the age of about six or seven years old. And they decided maybe I ought to learn an instrument. By that time they’d observed that I was a lot interested in music, because I would do this on my own.
Let me ask you something about — you used the term “family piano,” in that the way families entertained themselves back then were obviously different than now.
And was the piano a thing of luxury?

Well in those days we didn’t have television at all so we had to think of other things to entertain ourselves in the evening hours. And of course also the real popular thing was the radio. But we spent probably as much time or maybe more time, just with the music that we got out of the piano, and in later years I took up the violin when I was about six or seven years old. So I would do my thing on the violin. I got to where I could read the sheet music and I’d do that. My father played the bass fiddle and also the cello. So we’d just go through the stack of music quite often in the evenings. And that’s really where I learned a lot of music, by memory. Because we did this so often that it just sort of stuck with me.
Well that’s a great place to learn it. And hearing the other instruments with you, too, is valuable.
